content: Chondrodermatitis nodularis chronica helicis (CNCH) was first identified in 1915 by dermatologist Max Winkler, who described it in a paper titled Knötchenförmige Erkrankung am Helix. In 1925, Foerster expanded on the clinical, microscopic, and therapeutic aspects of the condition. The pathophysiology of CNCH remains unclear. It is thought to result from chronic pressure on the helix of the ear, leading to an inflammatory condition. However, it can also occur on the anti-helix. CNCH is most commonly observed in elderly men, though it has been reported in women and younger individuals, particularly when associated with autoimmune or connective tissue disorders. The anatomy of the ear pinna plays a role in the development of CNCH, as the pinna has limited blood supply and minimal subcutaneous tissue, making it prone to ischemia and necrosis under conditions of pressure, trauma, or exposure to cold temperatures. In 2009, the perichondrium vasculitis theory was proposed, explaining how these anatomical features contribute to the development of severe inflammation and cartilage necrosis, ultimately leading to CNCH. There is also evidence suggesting a potential genetic predisposition, as seen in a case study involving monozygotic twins. Grossly, CNCH appears as a sore or nodule, while microscopically, it is characterized by hyperkeratosis, parakeratosis, epithelial hyperplasia, dermal tissue damage, cartilage destruction, and dermal vessel proliferation. The causes of CNCH include chronic pressure, trauma, anatomical features, temperature changes, and actinic damage to the ear. Prolonged pressure, such as sleeping on one side, is the most commonly reported cause. Other potential causes include the continuous use of headphones, earphones, cell phones, or hearing aids. In some cases, the condition may be idiopathic. There are also theories linking CNCH to autoimmune disorders and connective tissue diseases, such as scleroderma, autoimmune thyroiditis, lupus erythematosus, and dermatomyositis. CNCH typically presents as a painful nodular lesion with a central crust, which must be differentiated from basal cell carcinoma, a generally painless lesion with greater vascularity. Other conditions that may mimic CNCH include actinic keratosis, keratoacanthoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and gouty tophi. Epidemiologically, CNCH is more common than reported. It is most frequently observed in individuals aged 50–80 years but can also occur in younger adults and children. Unilateral lesions are more common than bilateral ones. The condition predominantly affects elderly men but can also be seen in women and children. There is no racial predilection, though it is more commonly observed in fair-skinned individuals with significant sun exposure. Risk factors for CNCH include pressure, trauma, sun damage, and systemic conditions. The natural history of CNCH begins with the development of a painful sore, which rarely resolves spontaneously. With treatment, the prognosis is generally good, though long-term morbidity is common. Remissions may occur if the condition is undertreated. Clinically, CNCH presents as a spontaneously appearing, round-to-oval, tender nodule with raised edges and a central crust or ulcer, typically on the helix or anti-helix of the ear. It is often found on the side of the ear that the patient sleeps on and is associated with nocturnal pain. While this is the most common presentation, bilateral lesions or diurnal pain may also occur. The lesion usually grows to a maximum size and then stabilizes. Physical examination findings are consistent with the clinical description of CNCH. There are no specific laboratory findings associated with the condition, but a skin biopsy may be necessary to differentiate it from carcinomatous lesions. Additional diagnostic studies may be warranted to investigate underlying systemic illnesses, such as autoimmune or connective tissue diseases, that may be associated with CNCH. Treatment options for CNCH include medical therapy and surgery. Surgical procedures, such as cartilage excision, curettage, and wedge excision, are considered the gold standard, with success rates ranging from 89% to 96% for wedge excision. Medical or conservative therapy focuses on eliminating triggers, such as pressure, trauma, or solar damage. Pressure-relieving prostheses, such as foam sponges, foam bandages, donut pillows, or CNCH pillows, are cost-effective options. Intralesional and topical steroids may be used as a second-line treatment, with a success rate of 30–40%, particularly for initial symptom relief. Local collagen injections can provide cushioning and correct contour deformities. Topical antibiotics are used to treat secondary bacterial infections. Carbon dioxide laser vaporization of the nodule and underlying cartilage has shown a 92% cure rate in one study, with immediate pain relief and excellent cosmetic results. Nitroglycerin gel has been used to reverse cartilage necrosis by vasodilating arteriolar smooth muscles. Photodynamic therapy improves blood flow to the lesion and exerts a cytotoxic effect. Preventive measures for CNCH include avoiding pressure on the ear and employing pressure-offloading techniques.
